Sample text:
---
There is a specific kind of quiet magic hidden inside used books—not in the stories printed by the publisher, capability-tested and mass-produced, but in the accidental artifacts left behind by the people who owned them before.

Historians and bibliophiles call it *marginalia*: the scribbles, underlines, exclamation points, and doodles crowded into the white borders of a page. When you buy a brand-new book, you are entering a private conversation between yourself and the author. When you pick up a battered paperback from a thrift store shelf, you are walking into a crowded room across time.

I find something deeply comforting about the way strangers haunt old pages. 

Sometimes, the ghosts are academic. You’ll open a worn copy of *The Great Gatsby* and find frantic, color-coded highlighting from a high school sophomore in 1998, desperately tracking the symbolism of the green light for an essay due the next morning. Halfway through chapter four, the highlighting abruptly stops. You are left to wonder: Did they give up? Did they drop the class? Did they fall so deeply into the story that they forgot to study it?

Other times, the ghosts are intensely personal. A single sentence about grief or unrequited love will be underlined twice in heavy, trembling ballpoint pen, no notes attached. You read the sentence, and then you look at the ink, and suddenly you feel a sharp pang of empathy for someone you will never meet. You don't know their name, what decade they lived in, or who broke their heart, yet for three seconds on a Tuesday afternoon, you are standing in the exact emotional footprint they left behind.

And then there are the forgotten bookmarks—the mundane detritus of human life pressed flat between chapters. Grocery lists written on the backs of envelopes (*milk, lemons, stamps, call Mom*). Boarding passes for flights that landed twenty years ago. Polaroids of smiling people standing in front of cars they no longer drive. Receipts from diners that have since been torn down. 

We spend so much of our lives worrying about legacy, wondering if we will be remembered or if we are making a big enough dent in the universe. Yet some of the most intimate, enduring proof of our existence ends up being entirely accidental. It’s the coffee ring on page forty-two. It’s the dog-eared corner marking a favorite joke. It’s the inscription inside the front cover: *To Sarah, happy 23rd birthday, hope this makes the train rides go faster. Love, Dad.*

Even if the book eventually ends up in a dusty bin for a dollar, the love in that inscription doesn't evaporate. It just waits quietly in the dark, pressed between cardboard and glue, ready to remind the next person who opens it that humans have always been here—reading, underlining, buying lemons, and trying to make sense of it all.
---
